target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers and boost turnout
objection: A federal holiday would not reliably remove the barriers for low-income workers, because private employers generally are not required to provide paid time off on federal holidays and many retail, food service, healthcare support, and gig-adjacent workers would still have to work or lose pay/job security.

target: AG1's implication that a holiday by itself is an effective turnout solution
objection: Research suggests that making Election Day a holiday, on its own, is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms such as early voting, vote-by-mail, or easier registration.

target: AG2's assumption that because a holiday may not guarantee paid leave, it is therefore ineffective as access reform
objection: Even without guaranteed pay, a holiday still reduces practical friction by closing schools and many government services, changing transit schedules, easing childcare and family logistics, and making voting more compatible with daily routines.

target: AG2's argument that a holiday is not worthwhile because it is insufficient on its own
objection: Saying a holiday alone is not enough does not refute it as a useful reform; it can be paired with other measures like expanded early voting, vote-by-mail, streamlined registration, and employer time-off rules to remove one major barrier: time pressure.

target: AG1's claim that school, transit, and other logistical changes make a holiday meaningfully helpful for workers
objection: Those logistical changes do not solve the key problem for low-income workers, because many essential or customer-facing jobs still run, so the main obstacle remains whether workers can actually get paid or flexible time away from work to vote.

target: AG1's suggestion that a holiday can be added on top of other reforms without downside
objection: Making Election Day a holiday could be redundant and distracting if the real fixes are employer time-off rules, expanded early voting, and registration improvements; the holiday does not directly solve those problems and can pull attention away from them.

target: AG1's appeal to nationwide uniformity as a reason to prefer a federal holiday
objection: A uniform calendar does not create uniform worker protection, because private employers still would not be uniformly required to give paid or flexible time off, so the core constraint still varies by job and workplace.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday won't reliably help because many workers still have to work
objection: A national holiday still changes the default schedule for many employers, and because many businesses close or reduce hours on federal holidays, it removes the scheduling conflict for a large share of workers even if it is not universal.

target: AG2's argument that a holiday is not a strong enough reform unless it solves every barrier
objection: The fact that a holiday is not a complete solution does not make it unhelpful or ineffective; it is still a meaningful access improvement and can be part of a broader package of voting reforms.

target: AG2's claim that federal uniformity does not help because employer behavior still varies
objection: Uniformity of the holiday itself matters because it provides a consistent nationwide standard that reduces scheduling barriers across states, instead of leaving access entirely to patchwork local rules.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday reduces time pressure by changing schedules and logistics
objection: For low-wage workers the binding constraint is still whether they are scheduled to work during voting hours or can take paid/flexible time, so school or transit changes do not reliably give them actual voting time.

target: AG1's argument that a holiday complements other reforms rather than substituting for them
objection: A holiday can dilute pressure for the enforceable reforms that actually protect workers, because once Election Day is labeled a holiday, policymakers may treat the problem as solved and fail to adopt stronger time-off or early-voting protections.

target: AG1's claim that a federal holiday creates uniform access
objection: A national holiday only creates a uniform calendar change, not uniform employer obligations, so the key variable—whether an hourly worker can actually take time off—still depends on the workplace.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is too blunt because it will not guarantee paid time off for every worker
objection: Many employers close or reduce hours on federal holidays, so the policy changes the default schedule and removes the workday conflict for many workers even if paid leave is not guaranteed everywhere.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday would distract from better reforms
objection: Opposing the holiday because it is not the only solution is too demanding; supporting it does not prevent stronger reforms from also being enacted, and it can be an incremental improvement rather than a replacement for other measures.

target: AG2's concern that a holiday would not reduce waiting or election congestion
objection: A national holiday can actually help polling operations by giving jurisdictions more flexibility to staff polls and manage turnout without competing with normal school and work schedules, which may reduce practical barriers like long lines.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday changes the default schedule enough to help workers
objection: Essential and service jobs still run on holidays, so the core constraint for low-income hourly workers remains whether they can safely leave work or receive paid/flexible time; a holiday does not reliably change that reality.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday reduces time pressure and logistics overall
objection: A holiday can concentrate voting demand on one day, which may increase lines and waiting times at polling places and shift the time squeeze from work schedules to polling-place congestion.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday is a worthwhile incremental step
objection: Making a federal calendar change the headline policy misallocates effort when more direct levers—state time-off-to-vote rules, expanded early voting or vote-by-mail, and streamlined administration—address the binding constraint more effectively.

target: AG2's claim that some workers still having to work defeats the holiday's value
objection: The holiday does not have to solve every worker's problem to matter; it can still reduce barriers for millions by making voting more compatible with school and workplace schedules.

target: AG2's argument that congestion makes a holiday counterproductive
objection: Even if turnout is concentrated on the holiday, election administrators can better staff polling places and voters are less constrained by after-work and school-related timing, so the system can manage the day more effectively.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday would distract from stronger reforms
objection: That is an implementation concern, not a reason to oppose the baseline benefit; a holiday can be enacted alongside employer time-off rules, early voting, vote-by-mail, and administrative fixes.

target: AG2's assumption that a holiday cannot help unless it fully solves access
objection: A holiday can still reduce practical barriers such as line management and election-day operations, giving jurisdictions more capacity to handle turnout without competing with ordinary school and work congestion.

target: AG1's claim that better election administration and many workers benefiting make the holiday worthwhile
objection: Improved poll staffing does not solve the core time-off problem for low-income hourly workers, because they still need the ability to leave work safely and without losing pay; a holiday does not reliably provide that.

target: AG1's claim that the policy is acceptable because it helps many workers
objection: The distributional problem remains: a holiday may mainly help people with flexible jobs or jobs that close, while leaving inflexible hourly workers with the same constraints, potentially widening rather than reducing gaps in participation.

target: AG1's argument that a holiday is worthwhile when paired with other reforms
objection: If the holiday only matters when combined with enforceable time-off rules, expanded early voting, and administrative fixes, then it is an inefficient centerpiece compared with direct reforms that address the barrier without relying on a calendar change.
